objectives: Name the main parts of a desktop computer
Say what each part does
Tell input devices from output devices
Explain what hardware and software are
reviewNotes: Very basic wording for Form 1; check the sequence of topics against the official programme.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: What is a computer?
blocks.md: A **computer** is an electronic machine. It takes in data (**input**), works on it (**processing**), shows the result (**output**) and can keep it (**storage**). Computers follow instructions called **programs**.

blocks.title: Main parts
blocks.md:
- **Monitor**: shows pictures and text (output).
- **Keyboard** and **mouse**: send data in (input).
- **System unit**: the box that holds the CPU, memory and disk.
- **CPU**: the 'brain' that carries out instructions.
- **Printer** and **speakers**: output devices.

blocks.caption: A table of four computer parts and the job of each.
blocks.alt: Table: monitor shows output, keyboard types input, mouse points and clicks, system unit holds the CPU and disk.

blocks.title: Hardware and software
blocks.md: **Hardware** is the part you can touch. **Software** is the programs that tell the hardware what to do. A word processor is software. A mouse is hardware.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- The monitor is **not** the computer; the system unit does the processing.
- Do not call a file 'hardware'. A file is data.
- A mouse is an input device, not an output device.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Sort these into input or output: keyboard, monitor, mouse, printer.
steps: Input sends data into the computer: keyboard, mouse.
Output shows results: monitor, printer.
blocks.answer: Input: keyboard, mouse. Output: monitor, printer.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A student types a letter, sees it on the screen and prints it. Name the device used at each step.
steps: Typing uses the keyboard (input).
Seeing uses the monitor and printing uses the printer (output).

Protect yourself from health problems
Care for equipment
Start and shut down a computer correctly
reviewNotes: Health advice is general; a health professional may review. Check the school's own computer-room rules.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Computer room rules
blocks.md:
- Do not eat or drink near computers.
- Keep bags and liquids away from cables.
- Do not unplug cables or open the system unit.
- Report faults to the teacher.
- Use only your own account and keep your password secret.

blocks.title: Healthy use
blocks.md: Sit with your back straight, feet flat on the floor and the screen at eye level. Take a short break every 30 to 60 minutes. Look away from the screen to rest your eyes. Good posture helps prevent back and neck pain.

blocks.caption: A person sits upright facing a screen at eye level.
blocks.alt: Diagram of a person sitting straight in front of a screen at eye level.

blocks.title: Starting and shutting down
blocks.md: Switch on the monitor and the computer. Log in. When you finish, **save your work**, close programs, then use **Shut down** from the menu. Do not just switch off at the socket: this can damage files.

blocks.title: Important
blocks.md:
- Electricity can be dangerous: never touch bare wires with wet hands.
- Power cuts can erase unsaved work: save often.
- A strong password is long and mixed; never write it on the desk.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: A pupil brings a bottle of water to the computer room. What should the teacher say and why?
steps: Liquids must stay away from computers.
A spill can short-circuit equipment and may cause an electric shock.
blocks.answer: Leave the water outside the room.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Put the shutdown steps in order: switch off the monitor, save your work, choose Shut down, close programs.
steps: First save, then close programs.
Then choose Shut down; switch off the monitor last.
blocks.answer: Save, close programs, Shut down, switch off the monitor.

reviewNotes: Shortcuts shown are the common Windows/Linux ones.

blocks.title: Keyboard zones
blocks.md: The keyboard has **letter keys** (QWERTY layout), a row of **number keys**, **function keys** (F1 to F12), **arrow keys**, and often a **numeric keypad**. **Shift** types capital letters. **Caps Lock** keeps capitals on. **Enter** starts a new line. **Space bar** adds a space.

blocks.title: Editing keys
blocks.md: **Backspace** deletes the character before the cursor. **Delete** removes the character after it. **Tab** moves along. **Esc** cancels. Useful shortcuts: **Ctrl + C** copy, **Ctrl + V** paste, **Ctrl + X** cut, **Ctrl + Z** undo, **Ctrl + S** save.

blocks.caption: A sketch of the keyboard with function keys, letter keys, arrow keys and a numeric keypad.
blocks.alt: Keyboard diagram showing four zones: function keys, letter and number keys, arrow keys and keypad.

blocks.title: The mouse
blocks.md: **Click** (left button) selects. **Double-click** opens. **Right-click** shows a menu. **Drag** means hold the left button and move. The scroll wheel moves a page up and down. Keep your wrist straight and rest your hand lightly.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using Caps Lock for one capital letter; use Shift instead.
- Mixing up Backspace (before) and Delete (after).
- Two fast clicks that are too slow count as two single clicks, not a double-click.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: You typed 'Camroon'. Fix it to 'Cameroon' using the keyboard.
steps: Move the cursor after 'Cam' using the arrow keys.
Type the missing letter 'e' to get Cameroon.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Copy a sentence and paste it below. Give the shortcut keys.
steps: Select the sentence, then press Ctrl + C to copy.
Move to a new line and press Ctrl + V to paste.

blocks.title: File and folder
blocks.md: A **file** is a named piece of data stored on a disk: a letter, a picture, a song, a program. A **folder** is like a drawer: it holds files and other folders. Folders keep your work in order.

blocks.title: File names
blocks.md: A file name has two parts: the **name** and the **extension** after a dot, e.g. letter.docx. The extension shows the file type: .docx (document), .jpg (photo), .mp3 (sound), .txt (plain text). Choose clear names like Maths_Homework.docx.

blocks.caption: A folder My Documents with sub-folders Maths and English; Maths holds homework.docx.
blocks.alt: Folder tree: My Documents contains Maths and English; Maths contains the file homework.docx.

blocks.title: Managing files
blocks.md: Right-click a file or folder to find **Copy**, **Cut**, **Paste**, **Rename** and **Delete**. Copy leaves the original. Cut moves it. Deleted files often go to the **Recycle Bin**, where you can restore them. Save with **Save As** to choose the folder and the name.

blocks.title: Mistakes
blocks.md:
- Do not use names like 'new1' that you will forget.
- Do not delete files you did not create.
- Keep copies of important files on a flash drive.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: What is the extension in the file name story.txt and what does it show?
steps: The extension is the part after the dot: txt.
It shows the file is plain text.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: You saved photo.jpg in the wrong folder. How do you move it to the folder Pictures?
steps: Right-click photo.jpg and choose Cut.
Open the folder Pictures, right-click and choose Paste.

reviewNotes: Button names vary slightly between programs.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Word processor
blocks.md: A **word processor** is a program for writing documents such as letters, essays and notices. You can type, correct mistakes, change how the text looks (**formatting**), save the file and print it.

blocks.title: Formatting
blocks.md: Select the text first (drag the mouse over it). Then use the toolbar: **B** for bold, **I** for italic, **U** for underline. Change the **font** and the **font size**. **Alignment** can be left, centre, right or justified. Use **bullets** or **numbers** for lists.

blocks.caption: Three boxes showing text lines aligned to the left, centre and right.
blocks.alt: Three small page sketches with lines of text aligned left, centre and right.

blocks.title: Save and print
blocks.md: Click **File** then **Save As**, choose a folder, type a name and click Save. Use **Ctrl + S** to save again as you work. Choose **Print Preview** before printing to check the page. Press **Ctrl + P** to print.

blocks.title: Mistakes
blocks.md:
- Formatting does nothing unless the text is **selected** first.
- Do not press Enter at the end of every line; the text wraps by itself.
- Spell checking does not catch every error: read the text yourself.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Make the title 'MY SCHOOL' bold, centred and size 20. Give the steps.
steps: Select the title with the mouse.
Click Bold (B), then Centre, then set the font size to 20.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: You typed a list of items on separate lines. How do you turn it into a bullet list?
steps: Select all the lines of the list.
Click the Bullets button on the toolbar.
